# Alpha Mus: A Blue Beacon in the Southern Flyway

*The modestly bright star at the heart of Musca is more than a point of light: its catalogue clues place it among hot, evolving stars—and offer a straightforward target for southern-sky watchers.*

Some stars announce themselves with spectacle; Alpha Mus makes a quieter invitation. In the far-southern constellation Musca, the Fly, it shines at about magnitude 2.65—bright enough to find with the unaided eye from a reasonably dark site, yet easy to overlook amid the richer scenery around the Southern Cross.

Its coordinates make a precise guide: right ascension 12 hours 37 minutes, declination 69 degrees 8 minutes south. Enter those numbers into a planetarium app or set them on a telescope’s digital finder, then look low in the southern sky if you’re observing from northern latitudes. For southern-hemisphere observers, Musca is better placed; choose a clear, dark evening and let your eyes adapt before searching. A binocular sweep can help identify the star’s field, though binoculars are not needed to see Alpha Mus itself.

The star’s catalogue classification adds substance to that small, sharp point. SIMBAD lists Alpha Mus as spectral type B2IV and classifies it as a double or multiple star. “B2” identifies a hot, blue-white star; “IV” denotes a subgiant, a star classified as having moved beyond the main sequence stage. The multiple-star label is a useful reminder that a star can have companions even when the unaided eye shows only one point. The available SIMBAD entry does not give a separation here, so don’t assume the components can be split with an ordinary backyard telescope.

There’s also a distance estimate hidden in the star’s tiny apparent shift against more distant background stars. SIMBAD lists a parallax of 10.34 milliarcseconds. Taking the inverse gives roughly 97 parsecs, or about 317 light-years. That makes Alpha Mus a useful contrast with nearby stars: its light has travelled for centuries before reaching your eye, while its apparent brightness is shaped both by its intrinsic nature and by distance.

For a relaxed observing session, begin with the constellation rather than the individual star. Musca lies in the southern sky near the familiar Southern Cross region. Use a printed chart or an app to trace the outline, then confirm the target by its position and brightness. If the horizon is hazy, give the star time to climb higher; at such a southerly declination, it can sit uncomfortably low for observers far north of the equator. A chair, a red-light torch and patience will improve the view more than magnification.

The reward is not a dramatic color change or a cloud of glitter. It is the recognition that an ordinary-looking point carries several stories at once: a hot stellar classification, an evolutionary label, a measured distance and the possibility of unseen companions. Find Alpha Mus on a clear night, and the Fly becomes less a faint constellation drawing than a small address in the larger architecture of the Milky Way.

**Source:** [SIMBAD: Alpha Mus / HIP 61585](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=HIP%2061585)
